overview: The limitations of batch processing arise from its core design: it waits to accumulate a complete dataset and processes it on a schedule, which inherently delays results.

Key limitations include high latency / lack of real-time results, stale data between runs, large resource spikes concentrated in the batch window, difficulty handling late-arriving data, the blast radius of whole-job failures, and growing scheduling/dependency complexity.
Understanding these limitations is what tells an engineer when to choose streaming or micro-batch instead of batch for a given workload.
learningObjectives: Enumerate the limitations of batch processing and the design reason behind each.
Explain how batch handles (and struggles with) late-arriving data.
Decide when these limitations justify moving a workload to streaming or micro-batch.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: The limitations of batch processing are the constraints inherent to processing a bounded dataset as a single scheduled unit of work: unavoidable end-to-end latency equal to at least the batch interval, data staleness between runs, bursty resource consumption during the processing window, complexity in correctly incorporating data that arrives after a window closes, large failure blast radius for monolithic jobs, and orchestration/dependency management overhead.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think about getting your mail once a day. It's efficient, but if someone sends you an urgent message at 9am, you won't see it until tomorrow's delivery - that's the latency and staleness problem. If a huge pile arrives all at once, your mailbox overflows - that's the resource spike. And if a letter arrives just after the mail carrier leaves, it waits a whole day - that's late-arriving data. Those are batch's limitations.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Batch's latency limitation drove decades of innovation: nightly mainframe jobs gave way to faster ETL, then to MapReduce, but all shared the fundamental delay of waiting for a window. The desire to overcome staleness and latency directly motivated the rise of stream processing (Storm, Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Structured Streaming) and the Lambda/Kappa architectures in the 2010s that combine or replace batch to serve fresh results.

whyItMatters.business: Batch latency means decisions are made on data that may be hours old; for fraud, personalization, or alerting, that staleness translates directly into lost revenue or risk that the business cannot accept.
whyItMatters.engineering: Knowing batch's limitations prevents misapplying it to real-time needs, and shapes how engineers handle late data, size windows, and design failure recovery and dependency orchestration.
whyItMatters.scalability: Concentrating an entire day's processing into one window creates large resource spikes that must be provisioned for, complicating capacity planning and straining shared clusters.
whyItMatters.cost: Spiky demand can force over-provisioning to meet the window SLA, and reprocessing large failed jobs wastes compute - both undercut batch's usual cost advantage when limits are hit.
whyItMatters.reliability: A failure late in a monolithic job can require reprocessing everything, and incorrect late-data handling silently corrupts results - both threaten reliability if not designed around.

coreComponents.name: Batch Window / Interval
coreComponents.definition: The scheduled period between runs that determines how fresh outputs can be.
coreComponents.purpose: It bounds the unit of work, but it is also the direct source of the latency and staleness limitations.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Sets the minimum end-to-end latency; results cannot be fresher than one interval.
coreComponents.examples: A daily 02:00 run means data can be up to ~24h+ stale by the next cycle.

coreComponents.name: Late-Arriving Data Handler
coreComponents.definition: The logic (or lack thereof) that deals with records that land after their window has been processed.
coreComponents.purpose: To incorporate corrections without silently dropping or misattributing late records.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Reprocessing affected partitions, restating outputs, or buffering late events.
coreComponents.examples: A transaction timestamped yesterday that arrives after yesterday's job ran.

coreComponents.name: Orchestrator / Dependency Graph
coreComponents.definition: The DAG of scheduled jobs and their dependencies managed by a scheduler.
coreComponents.purpose: To coordinate ordering, but it is also the source of scheduling/dependency complexity at scale.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Resolving dependencies, retries, backfills, SLA monitoring across many interrelated jobs.
coreComponents.examples: Airflow DAGs where hundreds of tasks must run in the right order each night.

internalWorking: Data accumulates until the scheduled window fires, so any record's results are delayed by at least the time until the next run - the latency limitation.
Between runs, downstream consumers see only the last completed output, so they operate on stale data until the next batch finishes.
When the window fires, the entire accumulated volume is processed at once, producing a sharp resource spike that must fit within the SLA.
Records that arrive after their window closes are either dropped, misattributed to the current window, or require a reprocessing/restatement of the affected partition - the late-data limitation.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Data accumulates (staleness grows) -> Window fires (resource spike) -> Whole-job processing (failure blast radius) -> Output (latency = >= one interval) -> Late data forces partition restatement
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Transactions stream in all day, but the pipeline only runs nightly, so intra-day dashboards stay stale.
2. At 02:00 the full day's volume hits the cluster at once, spiking CPU/memory and shuffle.
3. The monolithic job fails at the 90% mark due to a bad record; the whole job must be rerun, doubling cost and risking the SLA.
4. A transaction timestamped 23:55 yesterday arrives at 02:10 today - after the window closed - so yesterday's totals are already wrong until a restatement reprocesses that partition.

keyTerminology.meaning: The delay between an event occurring and its results being available; for batch it is at least one window interval.
keyTerminology.importance: Batch's defining limitation - it cannot serve real-time needs.

keyTerminology.meaning: Records whose event time falls in a window that has already been processed.
keyTerminology.importance: Hard to handle correctly in batch; mishandling silently corrupts historical aggregates.

keyTerminology.meaning: The amount of work that must be redone when a job fails.
keyTerminology.importance: For large monolithic batch jobs this can be the entire dataset, wasting time and compute.

importantConcepts.explanation: Because outputs only refresh when a batch completes, every consumer between runs sees data frozen at the last run. For a daily job, decisions at 4pm use data that is potentially 14+ hours old, which is unacceptable for time-sensitive use cases.

The standard batch remedy for late data is to reprocess (restate) the affected historical partition with a lookback window - e.g., re-run the last N days each night so late events are eventually captured - trading extra compute for correctness, but with delayed accuracy.

variationsAndTypes: **Latency limitation:** Inherent to any scheduled window; mitigated only by shrinking the interval (micro-batch) or moving to streaming.
**Resource-spike limitation:** Addressed with autoscaling/elastic clusters, but capacity must still meet the window SLA.
**Late-data limitation:** Addressed via lookback reprocessing windows, watermark-like cutoffs, or restatement of affected partitions.
advantages: **High throughput:** (Context) Batch still excels at bulk volume, which is why these limitations are tolerated for the right use cases.
**Predictable scheduling:** Limitations are well-understood and manageable for periodic workloads.
**Simple recovery model:** Despite blast radius, idempotent reruns make recovery conceptually simple.
disadvantages: **High latency / not real-time:** Results lag by at least one window interval.
**Stale data between runs:** Consumers see frozen outputs until the next completion.
**Resource spikes:** A whole period's load lands at once, straining infrastructure.
**Late-arriving data is hard:** Late records require restatement or risk silent corruption.
**Whole-job failure blast radius:** Late failures can force reprocessing everything.
**Scheduling/dependency complexity:** Large DAGs are operationally heavy to maintain.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Accept batch's limitations when the business tolerates latency (minutes-to-hours), data is bounded, and completeness/throughput dominate - e.g., reporting, billing, ML training, reconciliation.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid batch when limitations are dealbreakers: sub-second to seconds freshness needs (fraud detection, real-time personalization, alerting, live dashboards), or continuous unbounded data that must be acted on immediately - choose streaming, or micro-batch when minutes are acceptable.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Batch is like a bus on a fixed timetable. It's efficient and cheap because it carries many passengers at once, but if you just miss it you wait for the next one (latency), the bus stop floods with people at departure time (resource spike), and someone who shows up a minute late has to wait for the following bus or be left behind (late data). A taxi (streaming) leaves whenever you need it, but costs far more.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can make batch real-time just by running it more often.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Shrinking the interval reduces latency but increases per-run overhead and scheduling pressure; below a few minutes it becomes micro-batch, and true sub-second freshness still requires a streaming engine.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Late-arriving data isn't a real problem in batch.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Late data silently corrupts historical aggregates if ignored. Correct handling requires lookback reprocessing or restatement, which adds compute and delays final accuracy.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Resource spikes during the window require autoscaling and careful capacity planning; shared clusters can suffer contention when many big jobs land in the same window.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Whole-job failure blast radius is mitigated by checkpointing, partitioning work into smaller idempotent tasks, and retries - but a poorly partitioned monolith remains risky.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Splitting jobs into per-partition tasks limits the rework when one fails; lineage recomputation and orchestrator retries help, but late failures are costly.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track freshness/latency lag, window-overrun against SLA, late-data volume, and failure/retry rates to detect when limitations are biting.
productionConsiderations.security: Long-running window jobs widen the exposure window for credentials; scope and rotate service accounts and isolate per-partition access.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Spiky demand can force over-provisioning; use autoscaling and spot capacity, and avoid reprocessing whole jobs by partitioning and lookback-only restatement.
productionConsiderations.performance: Window overruns cascade into downstream delays; tune partitioning, skew handling, and shuffle to keep runs within the window.

codeExamples.title: Handling Late-Arriving Data with a Lookback Reprocessing Window (PySpark)
codeExamples.overview: A common batch mitigation for the late-data limitation: each nightly run reprocesses the last N days using event time so late records are eventually captured and partitions restated.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
import sys

run_date = sys.argv[1]            # e.g. '2026-06-17'
LOOKBACK_DAYS = 3                  # reprocess a window to absorb late data

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("late_data_lookback").getOrCreate()

# Read by INGEST date (when data landed), but aggregate by EVENT date.
# Late events ingested today but timestamped earlier are thus captured.
start = F.date_sub(F.lit(run_date), LOOKBACK_DAYS)
events = (spark.read.parquet("s3://raw/events")
    .where((F.col("ingest_dt") >= start) & (F.col("ingest_dt") <= F.lit(run_date))))

# Aggregate by event date so a late record lands in its correct day
restated = (events
    .withColumn("event_dt", F.to_date("event_ts"))
    .groupBy("event_dt")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))

# Restate (overwrite) only the affected event-date partitions
(restated.write
    .mode("overwrite")
    .option("partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")
    .partitionBy("event_dt")
    .parquet("s3://warehouse/daily_revenue"))

spark.stop()
codeExamples.breakdown: Reading by ingest date but grouping by event date lets late records (ingested today, timestamped earlier) be re-attributed to their true day. Dynamic partition overwrite restates only the affected event-date partitions, fixing aggregates without duplicates.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Daily revenue partitions for the last few event dates are restated to include late records, correcting previously published totals.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Choosing too small a lookback misses very late data; partitioning by ingest date instead of event date misattributes late records to the wrong day.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Set lookback from observed late-data distribution; consider watermark-style cutoffs to bound infinite reprocessing; use Delta/Iceberg MERGE for efficient restatement.

codeExamples.title: Limiting Failure Blast Radius with Per-Partition Idempotent Tasks (Airflow)
codeExamples.overview: Instead of one monolithic job (large blast radius), fan out into independent per-partition tasks so a single failure only reruns its own slice.
codeExamples.code:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

REGIONS = ["us", "eu", "apac"]

with DAG(
    dag_id="region_etl_fanout",
    schedule_interval="0 2 * * *",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    default_args={"retries": 3, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)},
    max_active_tasks=3,   # control the resource spike concurrency
) as dag:

    # Each region is an independent idempotent task: a failure reruns ONLY that region,
    # not the whole dataset -> smaller failure blast radius.
    for region in REGIONS:
        BashOperator(
            task_id=f"etl_{region}",
            bash_command=f"spark-submit region_etl.py {{{{ ds }}}} {region}",
        )
codeExamples.breakdown: Splitting one big job into per-region tasks means a failure in 'eu' retries only 'eu', not 'us' and 'apac'. max_active_tasks throttles concurrency to soften the resource spike, and retries handle transient failures.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Three independent region ETL tasks run nightly; any single failure reruns just that region's slice within its SLA.
codeExamples.commonIssues: If tasks aren't idempotent, retries duplicate data; too-high concurrency reintroduces a damaging resource spike.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Size max_active_tasks to cluster capacity; make each task overwrite only its own partition; alert on per-task SLA misses.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A payments company runs nightly fraud-loss reporting via batch, but losses are mounting because confirmed-fraud transactions arrive late and the daily latency means the risk team reacts a full day behind.
endToEndExample.inputData: A day's transaction partition plus late-arriving fraud confirmations that can lag the original transaction by hours.
endToEndExample.architecture: Currently a single nightly Spark job. The example shows both the limitation (latency + late data corrupting daily totals) and a mitigation (lookback restatement), while noting that true fraud blocking needs streaming.
processingSteps: 1. Transactions accumulate all day; the batch only runs at 02:00, so intra-day fraud views are stale.
2. The monolithic job processes the full volume at once, spiking cluster resources.
3. Fraud confirmations timestamped yesterday arrive after the window, so yesterday's loss totals are understated.
4. A lookback job re-reads the last 3 ingest-days and restates affected event-date partitions to capture late confirmations.
5. The team recognizes that prevention (blocking fraud in real time) cannot be solved by batch and plans a streaming detection path.
endToEndExample.output: Eventually-correct daily fraud-loss reports after restatement, but with inherent latency - and a clear case for adding streaming for real-time blocking.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track late-confirmation volume, restatement frequency, window-overrun, and the gap between transaction time and report availability.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Idempotent per-partition restatement corrects late data; a failed monolithic run is split into smaller tasks to shrink blast radius on retry.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Batch is retained for accurate end-of-day accounting, but its latency and late-data limitations justify introducing a streaming layer for real-time fraud blocking - a textbook batch-vs-streaming decision.

industryUseCases.problem: Nightly batch fraud reporting cannot block fraudulent transactions in real time; by the time the batch runs, losses have occurred.
industryUseCases.solution: Keep batch for end-of-day accounting/reconciliation, but add a streaming layer (Flink/Kafka) for sub-second fraud scoring and blocking.
industryUseCases.benefits: Acknowledges batch's latency limitation and complements it with streaming where freshness creates value - a Lambda-style split.

industryUseCases.problem: Surge pricing and ETA decisions cannot wait for a nightly batch; stale data would misprice rides and harm experience.
industryUseCases.solution: Use streaming for real-time pricing/ETA while retaining batch for daily analytics, training data, and financial reporting.
industryUseCases.benefits: Each workload is matched to its latency need; batch limitations are avoided for real-time paths.

industryUseCases.problem: Large nightly inventory and analytics jobs create resource spikes and risk SLA overruns as data volume grows, and late returns/refunds arrive after windows close.
industryUseCases.solution: Autoscale elastic clusters for the spike, partition jobs to limit failure blast radius, and use lookback restatement for late refunds.
industryUseCases.benefits: Mitigates the spike, blast-radius, and late-data limitations while keeping batch for cost-efficient bulk processing.

productionDeepDive.scalability: The resource-spike limitation forces capacity planning around the window peak; autoscaling and spot fleets absorb the burst, but contention rises when many large jobs share a window, so stagger schedules.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Shrink the failure blast radius by partitioning monolithic jobs into independent idempotent tasks with checkpointing; orchestrator retries and Spark lineage recovery handle transient and node failures.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: HA centers on the orchestrator and metastore; long window jobs increase the impact of a scheduler outage during the run, so make the scheduler highly available and resumable.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Immutable inputs allow re-running affected windows in another region, but reprocessing very large jobs is slow - another reason to partition work for faster targeted recovery.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Address skew (the top cause of window overruns), tune shuffle partitions, use columnar formats and pruning, and split large jobs to keep each run within its SLA.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Avoid the cost penalty of reprocessing whole failed jobs by partitioning and restating only affected slices; use spot capacity and autoscaling to handle spikes without permanent over-provisioning.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Long-running window jobs widen credential exposure; use short-lived scoped tokens, per-partition access, encryption, and audit logging.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Alert on freshness/latency lag, window overruns, late-data volume, restatement frequency, and per-task failure rates - these are the leading indicators that batch limitations are hurting the SLA.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate that late-data lookback fully captures the late-arrival distribution; reconcile restated totals and flag silent corruption from dropped late records.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Centralize run-date-tagged logs; page on SLA breaches, blast-radius-large failures, and spikes in late-data volume that may indicate upstream delays.

recommendedPractices: **Match cadence to latency need:** If minutes/seconds matter, move to micro-batch or streaming rather than fighting batch latency.
**Handle late data explicitly:** Use event-time aggregation with a lookback/restatement window sized to the observed late-arrival distribution.
**Partition jobs to limit blast radius:** Independent idempotent tasks mean a failure reruns only its slice.
**Smooth resource spikes:** Stagger schedules and autoscale so one window doesn't overwhelm shared clusters.
engineeringStandards: Every job must define an SLA window and alert on overruns.
Late-data strategy (lookback or watermark cutoff) must be explicit and documented per pipeline.
Large jobs must be decomposed into idempotent, independently retryable units.
designRecommendations: Aggregate by event time, not ingest time, to attribute late records correctly.
Add a streaming or micro-batch path for the subset of consumers that need freshness, keeping batch for the rest.
Use table formats (Delta/Iceberg) with MERGE for efficient restatement instead of rewriting whole datasets.
namingConventions: Tag restatement jobs distinctly (e.g., daily_revenue_restate) so they are auditable.
Use event_dt partition keys to make late-data attribution explicit.
documentationStandards: Document the SLA, lookback window, and how late data is handled for each pipeline.
Record the failure-recovery procedure and the failure blast radius of each job.
Note which downstream consumers tolerate staleness and which require a streaming path.
testingStrategies: Test late-data handling by injecting records timestamped in already-processed windows and asserting correct restatement.
Chaos-test partial failures to verify only the failed partition reruns.
Load-test the window peak to confirm the job fits its SLA at projected volume.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using batch for a workload that needs real-time results.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Batch is the familiar default, so teams stretch it to use cases like fraud blocking or live personalization.
commonMistakes.impact: Latency and staleness cause lost revenue or risk; the business need is structurally unmet.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Identify the required freshness; if sub-second, use streaming. Keep batch only for the latency-tolerant parts.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Jobs aggregate by ingest time and assume all of a window's data has arrived when the window closes.
commonMistakes.impact: Late records are dropped or misattributed, silently corrupting historical aggregates and reports.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Aggregate by event time with a lookback/restatement window sized to the late-arrival distribution.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running one giant monolithic job with no partitioning.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Simplicity of a single job and lack of failure planning.
commonMistakes.impact: A late failure forces reprocessing the entire dataset, wasting compute and blowing the SLA - a huge blast radius.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Decompose into independent idempotent per-partition tasks so failures rerun only their slice.

comparisonSection.explanation: Batch's defining limitation is latency: outputs lag by at least one window and go stale until the next run. Streaming processes events continuously, eliminating this limitation at the cost of higher complexity and 24/7 compute.

Batch handles late data by reprocessing affected partitions after the fact, delaying final accuracy. Streaming engines use watermarks and allowed-lateness to update windowed results incrementally as late events arrive, handling lateness more gracefully but with stateful complexity.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the main limitations of batch processing?
beginnerQuestions.answer: High latency (not real-time), stale data between runs, large resource spikes during the processing window, difficulty handling late-arriving data, a large failure blast radius for monolithic jobs, and scheduling/dependency complexity at scale.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: List each limitation and tie it to the design cause (waiting for a window -> latency/staleness; whole period at once -> spike).

beginnerQuestions.question: Why can't batch processing deliver real-time results?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Batch waits to accumulate a complete dataset and runs on a schedule, so the minimum end-to-end latency equals at least one window interval. Results cannot be fresher than the last completed run.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Anchor the answer to the window interval being the floor on latency.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you handle late-arriving data in a batch pipeline?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Aggregate by event time rather than ingest time, and run a lookback window (re-read the last N ingest-days each run) that restates the affected event-date partitions, so late records are eventually attributed to their correct period. Size the lookback to the observed late-arrival distribution; optionally enforce a cutoff to bound reprocessing.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show event-time vs. ingest-time, lookback/restatement, and idempotent partition overwrite. Mention table-format MERGE for efficiency.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you reduce the failure blast radius of a large batch job?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Decompose the monolith into independent, idempotent per-partition tasks (e.g., per region/date), add checkpointing, and configure retries so a failure reruns only the affected slice rather than the entire dataset. Orchestrate with a DAG that retries individual tasks.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize partitioning + idempotency + targeted retry to limit rework and protect the SLA.

advancedQuestions.question: When would you choose streaming over batch, and what's the cost of that choice?
advancedQuestions.answer: Choose streaming when freshness creates business value at sub-second-to-seconds latency - fraud blocking, real-time personalization, alerting, live dashboards - or when data is unbounded and must be acted on immediately. The cost is higher complexity (watermarks, event-time skew, continuous state, exactly-once), always-on compute, and harder testing/recovery.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Frame the decision on latency value vs. added complexity/cost. Mention micro-batch as a middle ground for minutes-level freshness.

advancedQuestions.question: How do Lambda and Kappa architectures relate to batch's limitations?
advancedQuestions.answer: Lambda runs a batch layer for accurate, complete results plus a speed (streaming) layer for low-latency approximate results, merging them - directly compensating for batch's latency/staleness limitation. Kappa drops the batch layer and reprocesses everything through a single streaming pipeline (replaying the log), avoiding dual codebases. Both exist because batch alone can't meet real-time needs.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show you understand these patterns are responses to batch's latency limitation, with the trade-off of maintaining two systems (Lambda) vs. streaming complexity (Kappa).

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your nightly batch job has started overrunning its window as data grows, and late refunds are corrupting daily totals. What do you do?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Two limitations: resource-spike/overrun and late data. Address overrun by partitioning + autoscaling + skew tuning; address late refunds with event-time aggregation + lookback restatement.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Split the monolith into per-partition idempotent tasks with autoscaling to fit the SLA and reduce blast radius, tune skew/shuffle to cut runtime, and switch refunds to event-time aggregation with a lookback window that restates affected day partitions so late refunds are captured correctly.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design analytics for a platform that needs both accurate daily financials and a real-time activity feed, given batch's limitations.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use a Lambda-style split: a batch layer (Spark) for complete, reconcilable daily financials and ML training, and a streaming layer (Flink/Kafka) for the real-time feed. Serve fresh results from streaming and authoritative restated results from batch; handle late data in batch via event-time lookback.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Batch alone can't meet the feed's latency (its core limitation); streaming alone complicates exact financial reconciliation. The split adds two codebases but matches each need; Kappa would unify on streaming at higher complexity.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Partition batch jobs by date and stagger windows to avoid spikes; autoscale both layers; bound late-data reprocessing with a lookback cutoff.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Batch's limitations: high latency / not real-time, stale data between runs, resource spikes, hard late-data handling, large failure blast radius, and scheduling/dependency complexity.
keyConcepts: Outputs are stale until the next run completes.
Late data needs event-time + lookback restatement.
Monolithic jobs = large failure blast radius.
formulas: Minimum end-to-end latency >= batch interval + run duration; data staleness at time t = t - (timestamp of last completed run).
commands: airflow dags backfill -s 2026-06-14 -e 2026-06-17 region_etl_fanout  # targeted rerun of slices
interviewPoints: Latency is batch's defining limitation - know the window-interval floor.
Handle late data with event-time aggregation + lookback restatement.
Partition jobs to shrink failure blast radius.
Choose streaming when sub-second freshness has business value.
Lambda/Kappa exist to overcome batch latency.
quickNotes: More frequent runs reduce latency but become micro-batch, not true real-time.
Ignoring late data silently corrupts historical aggregates.
Stagger and autoscale to absorb resource spikes.
Idempotent per-partition tasks make retries cheap and safe.

keyTakeaways: Batch's core limitations are high latency / lack of real-time results, stale data between runs, resource spikes during the window, hard late-data handling, large failure blast radius, and scheduling/dependency complexity.
The minimum end-to-end latency of any batch pipeline is at least one window interval, which is why batch cannot serve sub-second use cases like fraud blocking.
Late-arriving data is handled by aggregating on event time and running a lookback window that restates affected partitions - mishandling it silently corrupts historical aggregates.
Shrink the failure blast radius and smooth resource spikes by decomposing monolithic jobs into independent, idempotent, autoscaled per-partition tasks.

When freshness creates real business value at seconds-or-faster latency, choose streaming (or micro-batch for minutes); Lambda and Kappa architectures exist specifically to overcome batch's latency limitation.
